sections.h2: Tax offices in Jackson and Raymond
sections.html:
Two county seats, Jackson and Raymond, split Hinds County into a First Judicial District (Jackson) and a Second Judicial District (Raymond). The tax collector, tax assessor and chancery clerk all keep an office in each. Property tax here involves three elected offices. Value comes from the assessor. Bills and payments go through the collector. Deeds, the appeal hearing process before the Board of Supervisors and delinquent tax collection belong to the chancery clerk. Doors open at 8:00 a.m. and close at 5:00 p.m., weekdays, with legal holidays off.

  • Tax Collector, Jackson: 316 S. President St., 601-968-6587. Raymond: 127 W. Main St., 601-857-5574.
  • Tax Assessor, Jackson: mail to P.O. Box 22908, 601-968-6616. Raymond: mail to P.O. Box 549, 601-857-8787.
  • Chancery Clerk, Jackson: 316 S. President St., 601-968-6508. Raymond: Main St. Annex Building, 601-857-8055.

Call before you drive, since numbers and hours can change. Each office has a page on the county site: Tax Collector, Tax Assessor and Chancery Clerk.

sections.h2: How the assessor values a house
sections.html:
Each year the assessor builds a list of all taxable parcels, puts a value on each, applies the state ratio and hands a certified roll to the Board of Supervisors. Parcel counts range from about 100 in Learned to more than 70,000 inside Jackson, for a county total above 106,000.

A Class I property, meaning a single-family home its owner lives in, is assessed at 10 percent of true value. A rental house or other real estate is Class II at 15 percent. Multiply true value by the ratio and then by millage to get the tax.

One quarter of taxable property is reviewed each year, so all of it is seen at least every four years. For a typical house, that means an appraiser driving by and comparing the house to the drawings and field sheet on file. You hear from the assessor only if the appraiser sees a difference from the file, and nobody has to enter your home. Sales ratio studies compare appraised values with real sale prices.

  • Deeds on file with the chancery clerk decide who the owner is as of January 1.
  • The roll reaches the Board of Supervisors on the first Monday in July.

sections.h2: Dates on the Hinds County tax calendar
sections.html:
February 1 is the due date for property assessed the year before. When that date is a weekend or legal holiday, the next Monday counts, penalty-free. Every December the tax collector mails the statements, and current taxes can be paid in three installments.

Hinds County property tax dates
DateWhat happens
January 1Whoever owns the parcel is the taxed owner for that assessment year
January 1 to April 1Window to file for homestead
First Monday in JulyBoard of Supervisors receives the roll
First Monday in AugustUsual last day to file an assessment appeal
November to DecemberBills go out
February 1Last day to pay without interest
Last Monday in AugustTax sale for unpaid taxes

Unpaid tax picks up interest of one-half of one percent a month after February 1, and part of a month counts as a full one. In unusual conditions the governor can push the date back by proclamation, up to 60 days at a stretch.

To get a hearing, go through the Chancery Clerk. The Board of Supervisors hears appeals, and the request usually has to be in by the first Monday in August.

Do not wait for August. An owner can sit down with the assessor about values at any time of year, and Mississippi Code 27-35-89 covers the formal appeal after that. Business personal property works differently: values are posted after the first Monday in July, review runs through July 31, and a formal protest has to reach the chancery clerk by 9:00 a.m. on that first Monday in August.

Evidence wins. Your own recent appraisal is the best exhibit, since the board looks at how fair and accurate the value is. A wrong square footage on the file can sometimes bring a refund for earlier years through the chancery clerk.

Unpaid tax puts the property up at the county tax sale, held the last Monday in August. With no bidder, it is struck off to the state. Delinquent taxes are the chancery clerk's to collect, and an older delinquent year must be paid before the current one.

Delinquent accounts get no installments and accept cash or a money order only, never a personal check. The owner may redeem within two years of the sale. After that, the property either matures to the state or the buyer receives a tax deed, and you no longer own it.

For property sold to the state, call the Secretary of State at 1-866-835-2637. Delinquent and tax sale lists are posted on the county site.

  • Redeeming means paying the delinquent taxes with statutory damages and interest.
  • Selling before the sale date lets you clear the taxes from the proceeds.
  • Waiting until after the sale still leaves redemption open, but only through the chancery clerk.

Selling with unpaid taxes is allowed, because the title and closing process clears them. The title search shows back taxes, mortgages and other liens, and the balance usually comes out of your proceeds when you close.

Order the search before any money moves. An attorney or title company can do it, but the chancery clerk's office may not search records or prepare a deed. Every deed needs the seller's notarized signature, a legal description with indexing instructions, and the names, addresses and phone numbers of sellers, buyers and the preparer.

A buyer who occupies the home before January 1 can apply for homestead exemption from January 1 to April 1, which lowers that year's tax. Selling for cash leaves the order of steps alone, since recording and tax still come first. It only removes the wait on a buyer's lender.

Older homes, inherited houses and rentals are common here. Probate and heirship questions belong to the chancery court, and the clerk files the papers. When the owner has died, title may need clearing before anyone can sign a deed.

The Tax Collector accepts cash, check or credit card with a 2.25 percent surcharge. Tags paid by personal check are held for 10 working days. Offices are at 316 S. President St. in Jackson and 127 W. Main St. in Raymond. Whichever you use, bring the statement or parcel number so staff can find the right account quickly.

sections.h2: The county and its housing market
sections.html:
Hinds County is in central Mississippi and is the state's most populous county, with 227,742 residents at the 2020 census. It covers 877 square miles. The cities are Byram, Clinton, Jackson and Raymond. The towns are Bolton, Edwards, Learned, Terry and Utica. Part of Jackson lies in Madison and Rankin counties, so check which county bills a given parcel.

Public schools are served by three districts: Jackson Public School District, Clinton Public School District and Hinds County School District. Population has been falling, from 250,998 in 1980 to 227,742 in 2020, with an estimate of 211,888 for 2025. That trend can mean fewer buyers per listing, and a clean tax record removes one obstacle to closing.

faqs.q: When are Hinds County property taxes due?
faqs.a: February 1, for the prior year's assessment, or the next Monday if it lands on a weekend or holiday. Later payments pick up interest of one-half of one percent a month.

faqs.q: Where do I pay property tax in Hinds County?
faqs.a: Visit the Tax Collector in Jackson (316 S. President St.) or Raymond (127 W. Main St.). Cash, check and credit cards work, and cards add a 2.25 percent surcharge.

faqs.q: What is the Hinds County assessment ratio for a home?
faqs.a: Ten percent of true value for a single-family home the owner lives in, and 15 percent for other real property like a rental. Combined county, city and school millage then applies to that figure.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Hinds County property assessment?
faqs.a: The first Monday in August in most cases. Ask the Chancery Clerk for a Board of Supervisors hearing, and talk to the assessor long before that date.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Hinds County house if I owe back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. Back taxes come out of your proceeds at closing through the title company. After a tax sale, the chancery clerk collects the redemption amount, and the owner has two years from the sale to redeem.
